newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Gulf Coast still magnet for foreign crudes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Gulf Coast still magnet for foreign crudes.

text.p: The U.S. Gulf Coast remained a strong magnet for diverse foreign crudes on Thursday, keeping domestic grades in the doldrums, traders said.

The May spread between West Texas Intermediate/Cushing and North Sea Brent widened by around 25-30 cents to $1.30 a barrel Thursday afternoon, encouraging transatlantic trade despite high freight rates.
"The arbitrage is probably open because people aren't going to find homes for their barrels in Europe," said a U.S. based trader.
Brent talk was muted as the market digested British Petroleum's sale of eight cargoes at dated-related prices to Shell. The cargoes load April 11-21.
It was still unclear what Shell intended to do with the Brents, although many traders speculated that the company would absorb much of the crude into its own vast refining system.
The North Sea benchmark was pegged around WTI minus $1.00 a barrel delivered into the Gulf Coast.
Other North Sea crudes continued to move swiftly. Statoil sold two Osebergs in the past couple of days arriving at the end of April.
The price was around WTI minus 90 cents to $1.00 a barrel, traders said.
A Gullfaks A cargo is still available at around WTI minus $1.00.
The influx of North Sea as well as West African barrels has deflated prices not only for domestic grades but also for short-haul barrels from Latin America.
A U.S. company is offering a Colombian Vasconia cargo for end-April loading at June WTI minus $2.50 a barrel into the LOOP.
Cusiana, also from Colombia, was bid around $1.70 and offered at $1.50, traders said.
